Accommodate

/uh-KOM-uh-dayt/ — spelling hook: it's roomy enough for two c's AND two m's · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To accommodate to adjust or make room in order to fit someone's needs or wishes.

The airline agreed to accommodate the stranded passengers by booking them on the next flight at no charge.

Worked Example

Two guests told the innkeeper they couldn't climb stairs, another needed a gluten-free breakfast, and a third asked for a late checkout. By evening she had rearranged the rooms, revised the menu, and adjusted the schedule so everyone got what they needed.

The innkeeper accommodated her guests — she adjusted her own plans to fit their needs and wishes. To merely 'tolerate' guests is to put up with them; to accommodate them is to actively change things for their benefit.

How Accommodate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

oblige

oblige: to do a favor or service for someone

adapt

adapt: to adjust something to suit new conditions

Antonyms

refuse

refuse: to say no to a request

hinder

hinder: to make things harder for someone

How Strong Is It? — allow → accommodate → indulge

allow vs. accommodate

allow vs. accommodate: Allow is weaker than accommodate — allowing something just means not blocking it, while accommodating means actively adjusting your own plans to make it work.

indulge vs. accommodate

indulge vs. accommodate: Indulge is stronger than accommodate — accommodating meets reasonable needs, but indulging gives in to every wish, even unreasonable ones.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ac- (ad-)

prefix — ac- (ad-): to, toward (Latin)

root — mod

root — mod: measure, manner (Latin)

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make (verb-forming) (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin commodus meant 'fitting, suitable' — com- (together) + modus (measure). To accommodate is literally 'to make fit to' someone: adjusting things to their measure.
